passages.title: Hormonal mobilisation of glycogen in the perfused liver
paragraphs: Livers were removed from fed rats and perfused through the portal vein with a buffered medium containing no amino acids, no lactate and no other substrate from which glucose could be made. Any glucose appearing in the effluent therefore came from glycogen already in the tissue. Glycogen was measured at the start and again after 30 minutes of perfusion, and is reported as micromol of glucosyl units per gram of liver. Glucose output was steady over the 30 minutes in every preparation.

Glucagon reaches the hepatocyte in the blood and binds a receptor on the plasma membrane. The receptor activates a G protein, which activates adenylate cyclase, and the cyclic AMP formed activates protein kinase A. Protein kinase A phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase, which in turn phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase b to the a form. The same kinase phosphorylates glycogen synthase and inactivates it, so synthesis and breakdown are never stimulated together. Insulin opposes these changes. Glucose 6-phosphate released from glycogen cannot leave the cell until glucose 6-phosphatase, an enzyme of the endoplasmic reticulum, has removed its phosphate.

Six preparations were compared: a control with no hormone; glucagon at 1 nmol/L; glucagon together with a cell-permeant inhibitor of protein kinase A; insulin alone; glucagon and insulin together; and a liver from a strain whose hepatocytes carry no glucagon receptor, perfused with glucagon. Every liver began the perfusion with 300 micromol of glucosyl units per gram (Table 1). Cyclic AMP was measured on a freeze-clamped sample taken at the end of the perfusion, and the share of phosphorylase in the a form was measured in the same extract by assaying activity with and without the allosteric activator that the b form requires. Lactate in the effluent was below the limit of detection in all six preparations, so none of the glucose released had been recycled through the tissue.

passages.title: Charging specificity and a proofreading site in a synthetase
paragraphs: The synthetase studied here attaches isoleucine to its transfer RNA in two steps: the amino acid is activated with ATP at the synthetic site, then transferred to the tRNA. Valine differs from isoleucine by a single methyl group, and the synthetic site cannot exclude it completely. A second, separate site on the same enzyme hydrolyses valyl-tRNA formed in error, leaving the tRNA free to be charged again. This editing site does not act on correctly charged isoleucyl-tRNA.

Three forms of the enzyme were purified: the wild type, a form carrying a substitution that inactivates the editing site, and a form carrying a substitution in the synthetic site. The specificity constant kcat/Km for activation was measured for each amino acid separately. Both amino acids were then supplied together at 10 micromolar, far below the Km of either, so that the ratio of the two specificity constants sets the ratio at which the two are activated. The fraction of mischarged valyl-tRNA that the editing site hydrolysed was measured in the same assay. Each enzyme form was finally supplied to a translation system making a reporter protein, and the protein was analysed to count valine residues sitting at positions whose codons specify isoleucine (Table 1).

Ribosomes in this system discriminated among transfer RNAs by codon-anticodon pairing alone, and the reporter protein was recovered in the same yield from all three enzyme forms. The transfer RNA used was the same preparation throughout and was supplied in excess, so none of the three enzyme forms was limited by the amount of its acceptor. Isoleucine positions in the reporter protein were identified from the gene sequence, and the residue actually present at each was read by mass spectrometry of the digested protein.

passages.title: A two-component system in bacterial chemotaxis
paragraphs: A swimming bacterium alternates smooth runs with brief tumbles that reorient it. Attractant binding to a membrane receptor is transmitted to CheA, a kinase held against the receptor on the cytoplasmic side. CheA autophosphorylates on a histidine residue using ATP and passes the phosphoryl group to an aspartate of CheY. Phospho-CheY binds the flagellar motor and raises the probability of a tumble, while CheZ hydrolyses the phosphoryl group from CheY. Attractant binding lowers the activity of CheA, so phospho-CheY falls and runs lengthen. Over the following minutes the receptor is methylated by CheR, which restores CheA activity, while CheB removes those methyl groups. Adaptation by methylation lets the cell respond to a change in concentration rather than to its absolute value.

Six strains were filmed in a shallow chamber. The share of time spent tumbling was scored in the absence of attractant, 10 seconds after a uniform step of attractant was added, and again 5 minutes later with the attractant still present. Each strain was also placed at the edge of a stable attractant gradient and scored for whether the population moved up it over 30 minutes (Table 1).

All six strains swam at the same speed during runs and carried the same number of flagella, so the differences in Table 1 reflect the signal reaching the motor rather than the motor itself. The attractant was added as a uniform step throughout the chamber, so during the first measurement no strain faced a gradient and every cell experienced the same concentration. The strain in which the aspartate of CheY was replaced by alanine made the protein at the wild-type level, as judged by immunoblotting of whole-cell extracts.

passages.title: Sodium along the nephron and a loop diuretic
paragraphs: Sodium is filtered freely at the glomerulus, so the amount entering the tubule each minute is the product of the glomerular filtration rate and the plasma sodium concentration. At a filtration rate of 125 mL/min and a plasma sodium concentration of 140 mmol/L the filtered load is 17.5 mmol/min, and almost all of it is reclaimed. The proximal tubule takes back about 65%, driven by the sodium gradient that the sodium-potassium ATPase maintains at the basolateral membrane. The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle takes a further 25% through a cotransporter that carries one sodium ion, one potassium ion and two chloride ions together from lumen to cell; because this segment moves salt without water, it makes the medullary interstitium hyperosmotic and so allows the collecting duct to concentrate the urine. The distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct account for most of the rest (Figure 1).

Eight healthy volunteers on a fixed sodium intake were studied. Urine was collected for one hour before a single oral dose of compound NX-7, an inhibitor of the thick ascending limb cotransporter, and again during the fourth hour after it. Before the dose the group passed urine at 1.0 mL/min containing sodium at 175 mmol/L and potassium at 50 mmol/L, with an osmolality of 720 mOsm/kg of water. During the fourth hour after the dose urine flow was 10.0 mL/min, urine sodium was 105 mmol/L, urine potassium was 20 mmol/L and urine osmolality was 300 mOsm/kg of water, close to that of plasma. The glomerular filtration rate was 125 mL/min on both occasions, and plasma sodium fell from 140 to 139 mmol/L.
No volunteer was allowed to drink during the study, so the water lost in the urine was not replaced.

passages.title: Two clotting assays and an oral anticoagulant
paragraphs: Clotting is a cascade of proteolytic activations. In the tissue factor route, tissue factor exposed by injury binds factor VII and the pair activates factor X. In the contact route, factor XII activated on a surface activates factor XI, which activates factor IX; factor IX with factor VIII as its cofactor then activates factor X. From factor X onward the two routes share a common path: activated factor X with factor V converts prothrombin to thrombin, and thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin. Factors II, VII, IX and X each carry glutamate residues that are carboxylated in a reaction requiring reduced vitamin K, and the carboxylated residues let the factor bind calcium and dock on the membrane surface where it works.

Two assays were used. The prothrombin time adds tissue factor and calcium to citrated plasma and reports the time to a clot, so it depends on the tissue factor route and the common path. The activated partial thromboplastin time adds a surface activator and a phospholipid instead, so it depends on the contact route and the common path. Each sample was also mixed in equal volume with plasma from a healthy control and the activated partial thromboplastin time measured again: a sample short of a factor is corrected by the factor that control plasma supplies, while a sample containing an inhibitor of a factor prolongs the control plasma as well.

Four samples were tested blind (Table 1). One came from a person with a hereditary deficiency of factor VIII, one from a person with a hereditary deficiency of factor VII, one from a person who had developed an antibody against factor VIII, and one from a volunteer who had taken compound AV-3, an inhibitor of the reductase that regenerates reduced vitamin K, for four days. The reference interval is 11 to 13 seconds for the prothrombin time and 25 to 35 seconds for the activated partial thromboplastin time.

passages.title: Two routes into apoptosis in one cell line
paragraphs: Two routes lead a cell into apoptosis. In the intrinsic route, damage inside the cell drives BAX and BAK to permeabilise the mitochondrial outer membrane; cytochrome c escapes into the cytosol, where it nucleates an apoptosome with Apaf-1 that activates procaspase-9. Bcl-2 opposes BAX and BAK at that membrane. In the extrinsic route, a death ligand binds a death receptor at the surface and a complex assembles on the receptor tail that activates procaspase-8. Both initiator caspases then cleave procaspase-3, the executioner that cuts the several hundred substrates whose loss gives apoptosis its appearance.

Five lines derived from one parental line were used: the parental line, a line overexpressing Bcl-2, and lines in which caspase-9, caspase-8 or caspase-3 had been knocked out. Each was treated for 12 hours either with a DNA-damaging agent or with a soluble death ligand, and the share of cells showing apoptotic nuclei was scored. Cytochrome c in the cytosol was measured on a separate sample taken 4 hours after the DNA-damaging agent, once mitochondria had been removed by centrifugation (Table 1).

Every line grew at the same rate when untreated, and untreated parental cells scored 3% apoptotic with 5 arbitrary units of cytosolic cytochrome c. The amount of cytochrome c held in the mitochondria before treatment was the same in all five lines, as was the amount of death receptor at the surface. Each knockout was made by disrupting both copies of the gene, and no protein could be detected for the disrupted gene in the line that carried it. The DNA-damaging agent and the death ligand were each used at a concentration that gave the largest response in the parental line, so no result reflects a dose too low to act.

passages.title: Telomere length and the replicative limit in culture
paragraphs: A linear chromosome cannot be copied to its very end: the last primer laid down on the lagging strand leaves part of the overhang uncopied, and the end shortens at each division. The ends carry many tandem copies of a short repeat, bound by proteins that mark them as ends rather than as breaks. Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase carrying its own short RNA template, extends the overhang so that the repeats can be replaced. Most somatic cells express little or no telomerase, and when the repeats fall below a critical length the end is read as damaged and the cell stops dividing.

Three cultures of human fibroblasts were followed from one starting population. The first was left untreated. The second was given the gene for the catalytic subunit of telomerase, TERT. The third was given a version of that gene carrying a substitution in the active site that abolishes catalysis but leaves the protein stable and correctly assembled with the telomerase RNA. Mean telomere length was measured at intervals and the number of population doublings completed before growth stopped was recorded (Table 1). A dash marks a culture that had already stopped dividing.

Telomerase protein was present at the same level in the two transfected cultures, and no culture carried a mutation in the genes of the damage response that halts the cycle. All three cultures were split on the same schedule and the doublings counted from the number of cells recovered at each split. Averaged over the first 40 doublings the untreated culture lost 70 base pairs of telomere at each doubling.

passages.title: Reciprocal control at the fructose 6-phosphate step
paragraphs: Phosphofructokinase-1 phosphorylates fructose 6-phosphate with ATP; fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase hydrolyses the product back to fructose 6-phosphate and inorganic phosphate. Both reactions are strongly exergonic and neither is the reverse of the other, so if both ran at once the only net change would be the hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate. The cell avoids that by reciprocal control: fructose 2,6-bisphosphate activates phosphofructokinase-1 and inhibits fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase. Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is both made and destroyed by a single bifunctional protein carrying a kinase domain and a phosphatase domain. Protein kinase A phosphorylates that protein, and phosphorylation switches the kinase domain off and the phosphatase domain on, so glucagon lowers fructose 2,6-bisphosphate while insulin raises it.

Hepatocytes were studied in four states, with the flux through each enzyme measured separately using labelled substrate: a fed state with no hormone; after glucagon; after glucagon together with a compound that blocks the phosphatase domain of the bifunctional protein; and in a line engineered to express a phosphofructokinase-1 that does not bind fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, also treated with glucagon. Net glucose formed at this step is the fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase flux less the phosphofructokinase-1 flux, and a negative value means net flow toward pyruvate. The ATP consumed in cycling is the rate at which the pair turns with no net change, which is the smaller of the two fluxes (Table 1).
Flux through the other steps of gluconeogenesis was not limiting in any of the four states, and the cells' total ATP content differed by less than 5% among them.

passages.title: Two routes of peptide loading onto MHC molecules
paragraphs: MHC class I molecules are assembled in the endoplasmic reticulum and loaded there with peptides of 8 to 10 residues that the proteasome has produced in the cytosol and that the TAP transporter has pumped across the membrane of the reticulum. Class I is made by almost every nucleated cell and is read by CD8 T cells, so a protein made anywhere in the cytosol can be displayed. MHC class II molecules are assembled in the same compartment with the invariant chain filling the groove, travel through the Golgi to an acidified endosome, and are loaded there with peptides of 13 residues or more that acid proteases have cut from material taken in from outside. Class II is made by dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells and is read by CD4 T cells. The class II groove is open at both ends; the class I groove is closed.

A dendritic cell line was used in two ways: fed a soluble protein antigen that it took up by endocytosis, or infected with a virus that makes the same protein in the cytosol. A CD8 T cell clone and a CD4 T cell clone, each specific for a peptide of that protein, were added separately and the interferon released was measured. Four conditions were compared: no treatment; an inhibitor of the proteasome; chloroquine, which raises the pH inside endosomes; and brefeldin A, which blocks export from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi. A variant of the line lacking TAP was tested untreated (Table 1).

With no antigen at all the CD8 clone released 20 pg/mL and the CD4 clone 25 pg/mL. No drug altered the number of class I or class II molecules already at the cell surface during the 6 hours of the assay.

passages.title: Compatible solutes in a bacterium under salt stress
paragraphs: A bacterium in a medium of rising salt concentration loses water, and its cytoplasm must be brought back toward the osmolality of its surroundings if the turgor that drives growth is to be restored. The first response, within seconds, is uptake of potassium ions with synthesis of glutamate as the counter-ion. Potassium glutamate at high concentration interferes with the folding and the activity of cytoplasmic proteins, so it is only a stopgap. Over the following minutes the cell replaces it with a compatible solute, one that can reach hundreds of millimolar without disturbing protein function. The organism studied here cannot make glycine betaine but takes it up through a dedicated transporter when it is available, and accumulates it in proportion to the salt it faces.

Wild-type cells and cells carrying a deletion of the transporter gene were grown in a minimal medium to which sodium chloride had been added at 0.1, 0.5 or 1.0 mol/L, each with and without 1 mM glycine betaine. Without glycine betaine the wild type divided 0.90 times per hour at 0.1 mol/L added salt, 0.45 times per hour at 0.5 mol/L and 0.10 times per hour at 1.0 mol/L; with glycine betaine present the same cells divided 0.90, 0.80 and 0.55 times per hour. The deletion strain divided 0.90, 0.45 and 0.10 times per hour without glycine betaine, and 0.90, 0.46 and 0.11 times per hour with it. Internal glycine betaine was measured in cells grown with the solute present (Figure 1).

Both strains reached the same internal potassium concentration at each salt concentration, and the deletion strain regained the growth rate of the wild type at 1.0 mol/L when the transporter gene was restored to it on a plasmid.
